title.en: Homage in the drum and the weapons, on the roads, and in every kind of water

summary: Sixteen yajus of the same shape: one namaḥ, two names, each followed by ca. Rudra is saluted in the drum and its beating, as the bold fighter, the scout, the messenger and the envoy, as the bearer of sword, quiver, sharp arrows, trident and bow, then on the narrow path and the broad road. From the eighth yajus Sāyaṇa reads the names as Rudra in the form of water — in channels and falls, mire and lake, river and pond, well and pit, rain and rainless water — then as present in the cloud, with the lightning, in the clear autumn cloud and with the sunshine, and as the rain that comes with the wind and the storm-rain of the dissolution; the anuvāka ends with the homestead and its guardian.

vyakarana.note: From dundubhi ‘kettle-drum’ with -ya (the final i drops before it). A taddhita in -ya, ‘being in, belonging to’ (tatra bhavaḥ, P. 4.3.53); not a compound. The dative goes with namaḥ: ‘homage to X’ takes the dative (P. 2.3.16). So does every name in this anuvāka.
From āhanana (ā + √han) ‘striking; the drum-stick’ with -ya.

translation.literal: Homage [be] to the one in the drum and to the one in the drum-beating.
translation.readable: Homage to him who is in the drum and to him who is in the stroke that beats it.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa introduces sixteen further yajus of the same kind («षोडश यजूंष्याह»). The dundubhya is the sound in the drum: «दुन्दुभौ भेर्यां भवः शब्दो दुन्दुभ्यः». The āhanana is the stick with which the drum is struck («दुन्दुभ्याघातार्थो दण्डः»), and the āhananya is the one present in it as the striking: «ताडनरूपेणोत्पन्न आहनन्यः».

flags.note: corrections.json (N7.1): the second witness (W2) reads आहनव्याय; the text keeps W1’s चाहनन्याय, which Sāyaṇa’s gloss (आहनन्यः, from आहननं) confirms.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa begins here the names of water. He explains kāṭa as «कुत्सितम् अटति जलमत्रेति», ‘where water moves poorly’: «काटोऽल्पप्रवाहयोग्यः कुल्याप्रदेशस्तत्र जलरूपेण भवः काट्यः» — a channel fit for a small flow, and Rudra is present in it as the water. The nīpa is the place where water drops from a mountain-top («पर्वताग्राज् जलं न्यग्भावेन पतति»), and he is present there as the water: «जलरूपेणावस्थितो नीप्यः».

flags.note: īdhra is not in Monier-Williams; its sense here rests on Sāyaṇa (the autumn cloud, bright because clear). Keith renders ‘cloudy sky’.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: reṣma is the time of dissolution, when beings perish; reṣmiya is the rain-water of that time, with gravel and stones
stands after each of the two names: ‘to X and to Y’

vyakarana.note: From vāta ‘wind’ with -ya.
From reṣman (the dictionaries: ‘storm, whirlwind, storm-cloud’) with -iya; the dictionaries give the derivative as reṣmya, ‘being in a storm’. The Taittirīya text spells -iya.

translation.literal: Homage [be] to the one in the wind and to the one in the storm.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «वातेन सह वृष्टो वात्यः» — the one rained down with the wind. Reṣma he derives from the perishing of beings: «रिष्यन्ति विनश्यन्ति भूतान्यत्रेति रेष्मः प्रलयकालः» — the time of dissolution; the reṣmiya is the particular rain of that time, «शर्करापाषाणादिसहितो वृष्टिजलविशेषो रेष्मियः», carrying gravel, stones and the like.

flags.note: Monier-Williams gives reṣman ‘storm, whirlwind’ (after Mahīdhara, ‘the dissolution of the world’) and reṣmya ‘being in a storm’; Sāyaṇa takes reṣma as the time of dissolution and the reṣmiya as its rain. The translation keeps ‘storm’; Sāyaṇa’s rain of the dissolution is given in the word table and the traditional note.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: vāstu is the ground for building a house; vāstupa is its guardian

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

samasa.meaning: he who guards the house-site (-pa from √pā, ‘to protect’)

vyakarana.note: From vāstu ‘site, homestead’ (or, with Sāyaṇa, vastu ‘property’) with -ya, the final u taking guṇa and becoming av before y (as gavya from go): ‘belonging to the site, dwelling there’.

translation.literal: Homage [be] to the one of the dwelling-place and to the guardian of the dwelling-place.
translation.readable: Homage to him who dwells in the homestead and to him who guards it.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads vāstavya from vastu, possessions such as cattle and horses: Rudra is present there, «तत्र तत्कार्यरूपेण वा स्थितो वास्तव्यः» — or in the form of what they produce. For the second name he takes vāstu as building ground: «गृहनिर्माणार्था भूमिर्वास्तु तत्पालको वास्तुपः» — vāstu is the land for building a house, and vāstupa its guardian. With this the seventh anuvāka closes.

flags.note: Monier-Williams gives vāstavya ‘left on any spot (as a remainder; applied to Rudra, to whom the leavings of the sacrifice belong)’ and ‘resident’; Sāyaṇa derives it from vastu ‘property’ and makes it Rudra present in cattle, horses and the like. His gloss is partly damaged in the witness («वस्तु धनं(न)गवाश्वदि…»), so only its clear part is quoted. The translation keeps ‘dwelling-place’, which pairs with vāstupa.
